extracted.intended_audience: writers, journalists, editors, and anyone who composes or evaluates English prose (especially political writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for producing clear, precise English prose (with emphasis on political writing): identifies common faults and gives concrete rules and self-checks to avoid vagueness, pretension, and thoughtless phrase-mongering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staleness of imagery and lack of precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Two qualities common to bad modern prose: 'staleness of imagery' (worn-out, hackneyed turns of speech) and 'lack of precision' (vagueness or saying things that don't mean what the writer intends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abstract, hackneyed phrasing that replaces concrete images; do not let prose consist of 'phrases tacked together' or 'words chosen for ornament rather than meaning.' The writer should aim for concrete images and precise expression so that meaning is clear rather than vague or indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: DYING METAPHORS
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using metaphors that have become 'dead' or worn out and lost evocative power (Orwell's 'dying metaphors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a 'huge dump of worn-out metaphors' such as 'toe the line', 'play into the hands of', 'Achilles' heel', 'swan song', etc. Using such metaphors (or mixing incompatible metaphors) indicates a lack of genuine mental image and weakens clarity; invent fresh imagery where it serves thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPERATORS OR VERBAL FALSE LIMBS
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid padding sentences with general-purpose verbs plus nouns or adjectives that substitute for simple verbs — 'render inoperative', 'militate against', 'make contact with', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer single, specific verbs (break, stop, spoil, mend, kill) to noun-verb phrases; avoid turning verbs into phrases or overusing nominalizations. Watch for overuse of the passive voice, '-ize' and 'de-' formations, the 'not un-' construction, and stock circumlocutions ('with respect to', 'in view of', 'the fact that'). These devices pad sentences and mask weak thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRETENTIOUS DICTION
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dressing up simple statements with grandiose words of Latin or Greek origin, foreign phrases, or inflated adjectives to give a false air of scientific impartiality or culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't prefer Latin/Greek-derived words merely because they sound grand ('phenomenon, constitute, utilize') nor insert foreign expressions ('cul de sac', 'status quo') when unnecessary. Favor everyday English equivalents; avoid invented Latinate coinages that hide lack of thought ('deregionalize', 'non-fragmentary').

rubrics_metrics.name: MEANINGLESS WORDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using abstract or jargon words whose meanings are vague, variable, or effectively empty in context ('romantic', 'plastic', 'values', 'democracy', 'Fascism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of words that carry several incompatible meanings or serve as badges of approval rather than precise description. Do not use such terms to mislead: a writer who has a private definition but allows the reader to think something else is being dishonest. Tie words to discoverable objects or specific meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ready-made phrases and prefabricated idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on 'ready-made phrases' or 'prefabricated' strips of words that come automatically and construct sentences for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These phrases save mental effort but anesthetize thought and can partially conceal meaning even from the writer. Constantly guard against set phrases (e.g., 'lay the foundations', 'achieve a radical transformation') and jeer or reject worn-out idioms to prevent their spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concreteness over abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose concrete examples and vivid imagery rather than dissolving the concrete into vague abstract phrases ('success or failure in competitive activities' vs. 'race, battle, bread').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete detail typically communicates meaning more efficiently and memorably. When describing an idea, first form a clear mental picture or sensations, then choose words that precisely fit that image rather than starting with abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid euphemism and inflated style used to conceal insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Political writing often uses euphemism, inflated Latinisms, and vague phrases to name brutal or indefensible acts without calling up their true images (e.g., 'pacification', 'transfer of population', 'elimination of unreliable elements').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize euphemistic terminology and resist it — name things so that their mental image is clear. Inflated style is often a tool to blur responsibility or soften brutality; clarity exposes the moral and factual content of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrupulous self-questioning for each sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined writer should ask, for every sentence: 'What am I trying to say? What words will express it? What image or idiom will make it clearer? Is this image fresh enough to have an effect?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orwell suggests adding two more checks: 'Could I put it more shortly? Have I said anything that is avoidably ugly?' Use these questions as a habitual checklist to force precise thinking and eliminate stale expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orwell's six elementary rules for writers
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise set of practical rules Orwell offers: (1) Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print. (2) Never use a long word where a short one will do. (3) If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out. (4) Never use the passive where you can use the active. (5) Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent. (6) Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'elementary' rules demand a change of attitude; they are not exhaustive but will prevent most of the worst faults in the sample passages. Apply them flexibly (break a rule rather than produce something barbarous) and consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let meaning choose the word (avoid surrendering to words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the language and existing dialect rush in to do your thinking for you; instead, clarify the meaning first (often by mental images), then choose words intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put off using words until the idea is clear; then select the exact words that fit meaning and the likely impression on the reader. This prevents stale/mixed images, needless repetition, humbug, and vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cure specific fashionable verbal habits consciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Some bad usages and metaphors can be eliminated by conscious social action (Orwell cites 'explore every avenue' and 'leave no stone unturned' as phrases killed by jeers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively resist and ridicule trivial clichés; reducing Latin/Greek weight, foreignisms, and the 'not un-' formation is possible through conscious practice and critique. Individual habit change can slowly influence broader language trends.
